Legends to the Video
Segment 1. The patient at age 63. A postural tremor of the
outstretched hands and “no-no” head tremor were observed.
Segment 2. The same patient at age 71. Two weeks after the
left frontal cortical infarct, the patient regained almost complete
strength in her right arm but had mild weakness and sensory
deﬁcits in the right hand. There was no detectable tremor in her
right arm, but the tremor of the head and left side remained
unchanged.
Segment 3. When seen 5 weeks after the initial stroke, she
had a very subtle distal weakness of the right hand. There was
no detectable tremor in her right hand and signiﬁcant improve-
ment in her left hand and head tremor.

Antiamphiphysin-Positive Stiff-Person
Syndrome Associated With Small Cell
Lung Cancer

drome (SPS) has so far only been described in women with

breast adenocarcinoma. Here, we describe the rare case of a
female patient with antiamphiphysin /H11001SPS due to small cell
cancer of the lung. © 2006 Movement Disorder Society
Key words: stiff-person syndrome; antiamphiphysin-positive;
lung cancer
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurological disorder
characterized by progressive muscle rigidity mostly of autoim-
munological etiology, typically associated with autoantibodies
to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GADs). However, approxi-
mately 5% to 10% of cases are of paraneoplastic etiology
usually having breast adenocarcinoma
1-3 and are positive for
autoantibodies against amphiphysin. 4,5 Here, we describe the
rare case of a patient whose antiamphiphysin /H11001SPS was due to
a small cell cancer of the lung.
Case Report
A 56-year-old women presented with a 6-month history of
increasing muscle cramps and stiffness of both legs, trunk, and
inability to walk independently, and a 10-kg weight loss (see
Video). There was no weakness in the legs or arms, pyramidal
signs were negative, and cranial nerves were normal. EMG
(Fig. 1A) revealed involuntary continuous motor unit activity
(CMUA) in all affected muscles, including the truncal muscles,
without evidence for reﬂex spasms elicited by acoustic stimuli
and electrical peripheral nerve stimulation. Nerve conduction
studies were normal. Central motor conduction as measured by
transcranial magnetic stimulation to both arms and legs was-
normal, arguing against this being a spastic syndrome. Labo-
ratory results were negative for GAD antibodies but antiam-
phiphysin antibodies were highly increased (1:409,600),

adjacent to the right pulmonary hilus (arrows in B) and in the right frontal lobe close to the midline (arrow in C). Horizontal bar in A indicates 100
milliseconds. [Color ﬁgure can be viewed in the online issue, which is available at www.interscience.wiley.com.]

suggesting paraneoplastic SPS. No other antibodies were
examined. Cerebral spinal ﬂuid (CSF) analysis showed 3
white blood cells/ /H9262L, a protein of 38 mg/dL, IgG level of
27.8 mg/dL (normal /H1102134), and no oligoclonal bands, ruling
out encephalomyelitis.
6 Given a normal mammogram and
thoracic/abdominal CAT scan, a whole-body 18F-ﬂuorodes-
oxyglucose (FDG) PET was performed, showing two ex-
tracranial areas of increased FDG uptake retrosternal and
adjacent to the right pulmonary hilus (Fig. 1B). An addi-
tional area of increased FDG uptake surrounded by a de-
creased uptake was detected in central regions of the right
frontal lobe (Fig. 1C), later conﬁrmed by MRI suggesting
metastasis. Histology following exstirpation of the structure
within the right frontal lobe conﬁrmed metastasis of a small
cell lung carcinoma.
Symptomatic treatment of SPS was initiated with benzo-
diazepines and corticosteroids followed by causal cancer
therapy with cisplatin/etoposid and radiotherapy, which led
to a remarkable improvement of mobility during the follow-
ingmonths. The patient was able to walk independently for
short distances and stiffness was signiﬁcantly reduced (see
Video).
Discussion
This case presented with a typical history and clinical picture
of SPS, conﬁrmed by EMG. The rapid progression combined
with positive antiamphiphysin antibodies was suggestive of a
paraneoplastic disorder, which in SPS is usually associated
with breast cancer. Our case shows that small cell lung cancer
should be ruled out in patients with an antiamphiphysin
/H11001SPS
if there is no evidence for breast cancer. As in our case, GAD
antibodies are typically negative in antiamphiphysin /H11001paraneo-
plastic SPS. 7 Antiamphiphysin antibodies are a useful screen-
ing tool for a presumed paraneoplastic neurological syndrome
since they are rarely found in patients with cancer without a
neurological deﬁcit. However, they are not speciﬁc and may be
associated with a variety of different neurological syndromes
and tumors (Table 1).

Restless Legs Syndrome in Parkinson’s Disease
Patients May Improve With Subthalamic
Stimulation
Erika Driver-Dunckley, MD, 1
Virgilio Gerald H. Evidente, MD, 1*
Charles H. Adler, MD, PhD, 1 Renee Hillman, RN, 1
Jose Hernandez, BA, 2 Geoffrey Fletcher, MD, 3 and
Mark K. Lyons, MD 4
1Department of Neurology, Mayo Clinic Scottsdale,
Scottsdale, Arizona, USA
2Biostatistics Section, Mayo Clinic Scottsdale, Scottsdale,
Arizona, USA
3Neuroradiology Section, Mayo Clinic Scottsdale, Scottsdale,
Arizona, USA
4Department of Neurosurgery, Mayo Clinic Scottsdale,
Scottsdale, Arizona, USA
Abstract: We report on 6 advanced Parkinson’s disease (PD)
patients who underwent bilateral subthalamic nucleus (STN)
deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery whose restless legs syn-
drome (RLS) improved postoperatively. Despite a mean 56%
decrease in their levodopa equivalents postoperatively, their
RLS scores dropped by a mean of 84% (100% in three). Our
ﬁndings suggest that bilateral STN DBS surgery can improve
RLS in patients with advanced PD. © 2006 Movement Disor-
der Society
Key words: restless legs syndrome; Parkinson’s disease;
deep brain stimulation surgery
Restless legs syndrome (RLS) can affect up to 25% of the adult
population and may be increased in patients with Parkinson’s
disease (PD).
1,2 The pathophysiology is unknown but is
thought to be related to impaired central dopaminergic trans-
mission.
3 RLS in PD patients responds to the same dopaminer-
gic drugs used to treat PD. Reports are limited on the effect of
PD surgery on RLS symptoms, with one patient improving
